kid.question: What kind of message did the people ask the prophets to give?

options.text: Warnings that called them to change
Pleasant words even if untrue
News about the coming harvest
Songs for their worship

kid.explanation: The people asked prophets for pleasant messages instead of truthful ones.

kid.question: What happens to the wall in Isaiah’s warning?

options.text: It becomes a gate
It is painted white
It breaks suddenly
It grows taller

kid.explanation: Isaiah compares the consequences of rejected counsel to a wall that collapses and a vessel shattered beyond use.

kid.question: What did the Lord say would give His people strength?

options.text: Faster horses
Larger walls
More weapons
Quiet trust in Him

kid.explanation: The Lord offered salvation in returning, rest, quietness, and trust; the people chose flight on horses.

kid.question: What does the Lord promise to do when His people cry to Him?

options.text: Answer them
Hide from them
Send them away
Ask for payment

kid.explanation: The Lord waits to show mercy and promises to answer when the people cry to Him.

kid.question: What does the guiding voice tell the people?

options.text: Build a higher tower
This is the way; walk in it
Wait for a faster horse
Stop listening to teachers

kid.explanation: Even amid adversity, the people are promised visible teachers and guidance on which way to walk.

kid.question: What do the people do with their idols?

options.text: Carry them to Zion
Cover them with more gold
Throw them away
Ask them for rain

kid.explanation: The restored people reject their silver and gold images rather than continuing to honor them.

kid.question: What does the Lord promise for planted seeds?

options.text: A sudden wall collapse
A long drought
A new idol
Rain and abundant food

kid.explanation: The promised rain, abundant food, streams, and healing portray restoration after hardship.

kid.question: What happens to the desert in Isaiah 35?

options.text: It blossoms and rejoices
It becomes a city
It freezes over
It disappears beneath the sea

kid.explanation: Isaiah pictures a desert rejoicing and blossoming as part of the Lord’s renewing work.

kid.question: What message should be given to people with fearful hearts?

options.text: Hide until the harvest
Be strong; God will save
Make your own path alone
Give up on the journey

kid.explanation: The fearful are told to be strong because God comes to save; healing images follow.

kid.question: Where do the redeemed people travel on the holy road?

options.text: To Babylon
To the desert alone
To Zion
To a foreign throne

kid.explanation: The redeemed travel the way of holiness to Zion, where joy replaces sorrow.

high-school.question: Why was the request for “smooth things” a problem?

options.text: It made prophecy too difficult to hear
It asked prophets to speak in poetry
It put comfort ahead of truth
It focused on distant events

high-school.explanation: The people asked prophets for pleasant messages instead of truthful ones.

high-school.question: What do the broken wall and shattered pot together emphasize?

options.text: A strong wall can protect a fragile vessel
A clay pot can be repaired more easily than a wall
A warning matters only after visible damage
A hidden weakness can end in total collapse

high-school.explanation: Isaiah compares the consequences of rejected counsel to a wall that collapses and a vessel shattered beyond use.

high-school.question: How does the people’s answer about horses oppose the Lord’s offer?

options.text: They choose frantic escape instead of trusting return
They choose travel instead of staying in one city
They choose human teachers instead of prophets
They choose farming instead of fighting

high-school.explanation: The Lord offered salvation in returning, rest, quietness, and trust; the people chose flight on horses.

high-school.question: What does the Lord’s waiting in verse 18 reveal beside His judgment?

options.text: He has forgotten the people
He still intends to show mercy
He needs time to gain strength
He withdraws every promise

high-school.explanation: The Lord waits to show mercy and promises to answer when the people cry to Him.

high-school.question: What changes when the people can see their teachers and hear “This is the way”?

options.text: Hardship ends before anyone can learn
Teachers replace every personal choice
Guidance becomes available during hardship
Only one road remains physically open

high-school.explanation: Even amid adversity, the people are promised visible teachers and guidance on which way to walk.

high-school.question: What action shows a real change of allegiance in verse 22?

options.text: Repairing damaged images
Moving images to a safer place
Keeping images as a backup
Casting away once-valued images

high-school.explanation: The restored people reject their silver and gold images rather than continuing to honor them.

high-school.question: How do rain and the healing of a wound belong to the same promise?

options.text: Both portray the Lord restoring life after loss
Rain is a warning while healing is a punishment
Both describe the people’s military strength
Healing occurs only if rain stops

high-school.explanation: The promised rain, abundant food, streams, and healing portray restoration after hardship.

high-school.question: What does a blossoming wilderness suggest in this chapter?

options.text: A place of safety becomes dangerous
A place of loss becomes a place of life
A royal garden needs new workers
The people must abandon every dry place

high-school.explanation: Isaiah pictures a desert rejoicing and blossoming as part of the Lord’s renewing work.

high-school.question: How do the healings in verses 5–6 support the call to courage?

options.text: They show that fear is the only real problem
They make human help unnecessary
They picture God removing barriers that seemed fixed
They describe a new military campaign

high-school.explanation: The fearful are told to be strong because God comes to save; healing images follow.

high-school.question: What makes the highway more than an ordinary road?

options.text: It is wide enough for every army
It avoids every hill and valley
It leads to a new trading city
It represents a safe return for the redeemed

high-school.explanation: The redeemed travel the way of holiness to Zion, where joy replaces sorrow.

expert.question: What is the central failure in the people’s instruction to their seers?

options.text: They confused prophetic warnings with royal commands
They assumed judgment could only concern other nations
They treated a symbolic vision as a literal report
They tried to control revelation to avoid correction

expert.explanation: The people asked prophets for pleasant messages instead of truthful ones.

expert.question: Why pair a swelling breach with a vessel broken into unusable pieces?

options.text: The images move from delayed instability to irreversible ruin
The images contrast public danger with private safety
The images show that only the vessel, not the wall, was flawed
The images distinguish political defeat from spiritual renewal

expert.explanation: Isaiah compares the consequences of rejected counsel to a wall that collapses and a vessel shattered beyond use.

expert.question: What irony shapes the response to “we will flee upon horses”?

options.text: Their horses become the means of their return
Their chosen speed becomes the speed of their pursuers
Their trust in horses brings the promised rest
Their flight reveals that the threat was imaginary

expert.explanation: The Lord offered salvation in returning, rest, quietness, and trust; the people chose flight on horses.

expert.question: How does the Lord’s waiting reframe the preceding warning of collapse?

options.text: Delay proves the danger was overstated
Mercy removes any need for the people to return
Judgment does not cancel His readiness to be gracious
The warning was addressed only to foreign nations

expert.explanation: The Lord waits to show mercy and promises to answer when the people cry to Him.

expert.question: How do “bread of adversity” and a guiding voice work together?

options.text: Instruction is delayed until hardship has fully ended
Adversity proves the teachers were unreliable
The voice offers a shortcut around every consequence
Hardship remains, but instruction becomes accessible within it

expert.explanation: Even amid adversity, the people are promised visible teachers and guidance on which way to walk.

expert.question: Why mention precious silver and gold coverings when describing the idols’ rejection?

options.text: Costly appearance cannot make a false object worthy of trust
Precious metal had been the only source of the people’s sin
The images become acceptable once their coverings are removed
The coverings are offered as payment for rain

expert.explanation: The restored people reject their silver and gold images rather than continuing to honor them.

expert.question: What unifies the agricultural abundance and intensified light in this passage?

options.text: The images give a precise timetable for farming
Creation imagery conveys a far-reaching act of divine healing
The images praise the people’s new technology
The abundance cancels the passage’s call to return

expert.explanation: The promised rain, abundant food, streams, and healing portray restoration after hardship.

expert.question: How does the wilderness imagery answer the earlier vision of judgment?

options.text: The desert remains barren while Zion alone changes
The image shifts attention from God to human cultivation
The scene of barrenness becomes a sign of restored glory
The blooming scene denies that judgment ever occurred

expert.explanation: Isaiah pictures a desert rejoicing and blossoming as part of the Lord’s renewing work.

expert.question: What is the rhetorical role of opened eyes, unstopped ears, and leaping limbs?

options.text: They narrow the promise to three medical cases
They explain why the people first rejected the prophets
They replace the earlier command to strengthen the fearful
Concrete reversals make the promised salvation imaginable

expert.explanation: The fearful are told to be strong because God comes to save; healing images follow.

expert.question: How do the safe highway and vanishing sorrow complete the chapter’s movement?

options.text: They turn restoration into a secure return and lasting joy
They replace the need for holiness with a shorter route
They show that the journey matters more than its destination
They make hope depend on the travelers’ own strength

expert.explanation: The redeemed travel the way of holiness to Zion, where joy replaces sorrow.
